read.sections.0.text.source:
An object can be made in one place using ideas that travelled from somewhere else. Potters, traders, patrons and users all play a part in these connections. Shapes, patterns and materials can travel, while makers adapt them to their own skills and markets. A motif is a design or feature that appears again and again. Art history studies both the movement of ideas and local decisions.

The two real objects in this lesson were made in the fifteenth century. The first is a Vietnamese Plate with Peonies. It is painted with cobalt blue beneath a transparent glaze, a glass-like coating fired onto pottery. The Met explains that its flower motif reflects awareness of earlier Chinese traditions. The record also notes that Vietnamese potters competed for Southeast Asian markets with makers at Jingdezhen in China. The plate belongs to a regional story of making and trade, not to one isolated tradition.
read.sections.0.text.back:

Shapes, patterns and materials can move, while makers adapt them to suit their own skills and markets. A motif is a design or feature that appears again and again. Art history studies the movement of ideas as well as local decisions.

The two real objects in this lesson were made in the 15th century. The first is a Plate with Peonies (Plate with Peony Flowers) from Vietnam. This plate is painted with cobalt blue under a clear glaze, that is, a glass-like coating baked onto pottery. The Met explains that its flower motif shows knowledge of earlier Chinese traditions. The record also mentions that Vietnamese potters competed for Southeast Asian markets with makers in Jingdezhen, China. The plate belongs to a region's story of making and trade, not to one tradition standing apart on its own.
read.sections.0.text.note: "potter" is "perajin tembikar"; "pottery" is "tembikar", as Southeast Asia's TERMS. "glaze" is "glasir".

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Ideas can travel from place to place. A thing made in one place can use ideas from far away. Potters are people who make pottery. Potters, traders and buyers all help ideas move. Shapes and patterns travel. Makers change them to fit their own skills and buyers. A motif is a design that is used again and again.

Both objects in this lesson were made in the 1400s. The first is a plate from Vietnam. It has blue flowers called peonies. They are painted under a clear glaze. A glaze is a shiny, glass-like coat baked onto pottery. The museum says the flower motif shows the makers knew older Chinese designs. Vietnamese potters sold to buyers in Southeast Asia. Potters in Jingdezhen, in China, wanted the same buyers. So the plate is part of a bigger story of making and trade.

read.sections.1.heading.source: A jug likely made for export
read.sections.1.heading.back: A jug likely made for export

read.sections.1.text.source:
The second object is a Jug with Floral Scroll. The Met attributes it to Jingdezhen; an attribution names a maker, place or period on the basis of evidence. The museum says the jug's shape comes from Islamic metalwork, and thinks export was a likely purpose. Export means sending goods to another country or region to be used or sold. So a ceramic jug could combine Chinese making with a shape linked to another artistic setting. The museum's word "likely" matters. It shows an interpretation, because no surviving shipping record names the jug's first buyer.

The jug belongs to the Ming dynasty, which ruled China from 1368 to 1644. Ming decorative arts drew on earlier traditions and on contacts with West Asia. The emperor's court also used a design office to set standards for its own orders. Work directed by the court and work for international trade were different settings for artists. Both were part of the wider history of Chinese art. This background does not show that this export jug was made for the court.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The second object is a Jug with Floral Scroll (Jug with Flower Tendrils). The Met attributes it to Jingdezhen; an attribution names a maker, place or period based on evidence. The museum says the jug's shape comes from metalwork of the Islamic world, and considers export a possible purpose. Export means sending goods to another country or region to be used or sold. So a ceramic jug could combine the Chinese way of making with a shape connected to another artistic setting. The museum's word "likely" matters. That word shows an interpretation, because no remaining shipping record names the jug's first buyer.

The jug comes from the time of the Ming dynasty, which ruled China from 1368 to 1644. Ming decorative art used earlier traditions and connections with West Asia. The emperor's court also used a design office to set standards for its own orders. Work directed by the court and work for international trade were different settings for artists. Both were part of the wider history of Chinese art. This background does not show that this export jug was made for the court.
read.sections.1.text.note: "likely" is "kemungkinan" (in quotation marks, as the museum's word). "attribution" is "atribusi" (verb "mengatribusikan"), a museum term; flagged as hard for young readers.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
The second object is a jug with a pattern of flowers. The museum says it was made in Jingdezhen. Naming a place or maker from evidence is called attribution. The museum says the jug's shape comes from metal objects of the Islamic world. It thinks the jug was likely made for export. Export means sending goods to another place to sell. The word "likely" matters. It is the museum's view. No old record names the first buyer.

The jug was made under the Ming dynasty. This family ruled China from 1368 to 1644. Ming art used older ideas and ideas from West Asia. The emperor's court had a design office for its own orders. Work for the court and work for trade were different. This does not mean this jug was made for the court.

read.sections.2.text.source:
The two objects share blue painted decoration, yet they are not the same. Their shapes, materials and uses differ. Similarity alone cannot prove that these two vessels travelled together. Nor can it prove that their makers met, or that one was copied directly from the other. Those claims would need separate evidence. What the comparison does show is real, documented artistic connections across wider networks.

Exchange between cultures also takes place within histories of unequal power. The Met's record of the Vietnamese plate admits uncertainty about how blue-and-white pottery began in Vietnam. It discusses a link with the Chinese occupation of the early fifteenth century. We should keep that uncertainty. Influence is not always a simple, peaceful transfer, and local makers are not just passive receivers of ideas.

Vietnamese ceramics also hold many regional and cultural histories. A Smithsonian exhibition stresses the many ethnic traditions within modern Vietnam. It describes vessels for cooking, dining, storage, transport and ritual. It traces exports across Southeast Asia, and to West Asia and Japan, from the fourteenth century. So "Vietnamese" names a place, not one single style or use. Makers chose ideas and changed them for particular communities and customers. This adaptation, changing an idea for a new setting, is part of the story. Seeing these connections makes comparison more useful than sorting art into separate national boxes.
read.sections.2.text.back:

What this comparison does show is real and recorded artistic connections within wider networks.

Exchange between cultures also happens within histories of unequal power. The Met's record of that Vietnamese plate admits uncertainty about how blue-and-white pottery began in Vietnam. That record discusses its connection with the Chinese occupation of the early 15th century. We need to keep that uncertainty. Vietnamese ceramics also hold many regional and cultural histories. A Smithsonian exhibition stresses the many ethnic traditions within modern Vietnam. That exhibition describes vessels for cooking, eating, storing, carrying and ceremonies. That exhibition traces exports across all of Southeast Asia, and to West Asia and Japan, since the 14th century. So "Vietnamese" names a place, not just one style or one use. Makers chose ideas and changed them for particular communities and customers. This adaptation, that is, changing an idea for a new setting, is part of the story. Seeing these connections makes comparison more useful than sorting art into separate national boxes.
read.sections.2.text.note: "Chinese occupation" is "pendudukan Tiongkok", as Southeast Asia's TERMS ("occupation" = pendudukan). "ethnic traditions" is "tradisi suku bangsa". "Vietnamese" in quotation marks is "Vietnam", since Indonesian uses the country name as the adjective.
